## Biotite Multiple Sequence Alignment Part II

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Make sure you have the code from the previous page"}

This is the code to [fetch multiple genbank files and extract the protein](biotite_search_multiple.qmd) from the previous page. 

Make sure you have this ready as the code on this page follows on from the last one. 
```{python}
#| output: false
# Import biotite modules
import biotite.database.entrez as entrez
import biotite.sequence as seq
import biotite.sequence.align as align
import biotite.sequence.graphics as graphics
import biotite.sequence.io.genbank as genbank

# Target Taxon and Nuclear Gene
# Making them constants at the top makes them easy to change for different searches
TAXON = "Carnivora"
GENE = "MC1R"

# Query NCBI Nucleotide database 
query = (
    # Add search for taxon in "Organism" category
    entrez.SimpleQuery(TAXON, "Organism") 
    # & adds AND to search query - both must be present for the result 
    # | would add OR to the search query instead 
    # search for the gene of interest
    & entrez.SimpleQuery(GENE)
)

# Search NCBI nucleotide database (pulling 50 records)
search_results = entrez.search(query, db_name="nuccore", number=50)
print("Number of records found:", len(search_results))

# Fetching GenBank data from NCBI (using the first 30 records)
genbank_data = entrez.fetch_single_file(
    search_results[:30], # [:30] - stops after the 30th entry 
    None, # Don't specify a file path to save result to 
    db_name="nuccore", # Search the nucleotide database
    ret_type="gb" # Retrieve genbank file
)

# Collect all of the GenBank records together using MultiFile
genbank_multi_files = genbank.MultiFile.read(genbank_data)

# Make an empty dictionary to store each protein sequence
gene_sequences = {}

# Loop through the 30 collected sequences
for genbank_file in genbank_multi_files:
    # Extract the sequence as in the previous example
    organism_field = genbank_file.get_fields("SOURCE")
    species = organism_field[0].subfields["ORGANISM"][0]
    # Change spaces to underscores in species ID name
    species_id = species.replace(" ", "_")

    # Get annotated sequence - use try/except in case it is empty
    try:
        sequence_annotations = genbank.get_annotated_sequence(genbank_file)
    except:
        print("No sequence annotation found, skipping")
        # use continue to move to the next genbank_file in for loop
        continue

    # Find GENE CDS (Coding sequences)
    for feature in sequence_annotations.annotation:
            # Searching for a CDS record in the gene (contains the annotation and the sequence)
            # Checking that the feature is the gene of interest
            # Convert feature to string for a string comparison
            # .upper() to ensure the case is in upper case
        if (
            feature.key == "CDS"
            and GENE in str(feature).upper()
            ):

            print(f"Found {GENE}: {feature}")

            # Extract sequence corresponding to the feature
            # Should be gene of interest, CDS record
            gene_nt = sequence_annotations[feature]

            # Convert to an biotite specific DNA sequence
            gene_nt = seq.NucleotideSequence(gene_nt)

            # Translate using biotite translate function
            # Complete=True will translate the whole sequence
            # as one open reading frame (ORF)
            gene_protein = gene_nt.translate(complete=True)

            # Remove stop symbols
            gene_protein = gene_protein.remove_stops()

            # Convert to biotite proteinsequence 
            gene_protein = seq.ProteinSequence(gene_protein)

            # Make an id for the species and gene 
            seq_id = f"{species_id}_{GENE}"
            
            # add protein sequences to dictionary
            gene_sequences[seq_id] = gene_protein
```

:::

## 1. Pick a selection of genes to plot

We got 13 genes on the last step, if we put them all on a multiple sequence alignment plot it will be too messy. 

In the below example we make a new dictionary with only 6 sequences in. 

```{python}
# Choose 6 genes to plot on multiple sequence alignment
# Make a new dictionary
genes_to_plot = {} 
# Counter variable to count to 6 
counter = 0
# Use a loop to go through each sequence in the dictionary by the key
for seq_id in gene_sequences.keys():
    # Only add the sequence to the dictionary if there is less than 6 entries
    if counter < 6:
        genes_to_plot[seq_id] = gene_sequences[seq_id]
    counter += 1
```

## 2. Use align_multiple to do a multiple sequence alignment 

Biotite has a function called [align_multiple](https://www.biotite-python.org/latest/tutorial/sequence/align_multiple.html) which does a multiple sequence alignment. 

We can use this with our protein sequences.

```{python}
# Use align_multiple function from biotite align
# This returns four items, alignment, order, guide_tree, distance_matrix
# alignment is our aligned sequences 
# order is a suggested order, which groups closest related proteins together 
alignment, order, guide_tree, distance_matrix = align.align_multiple(
        # Provide the genes to plot as a list of sequences 
        list(genes_to_plot.values()),
        # Choose the matrix for the alignment 
        # Here it is the standard protein matrix 
        matrix=align.SubstitutionMatrix.std_protein_matrix(),
        # Gap penalty is how much a gap (e.g. insertion/deletion)
        # affects the final alignment 
        gap_penalty=-5,
)
```

## 3. Reorder the alignments, according to order

We can now use the suggested order from `align_multiple` to reorder our alignment. 

```{python}
# Reorder alignment based on guide tree and plot
# Print order to check what it is - an array of positions
print(f"Order is: {order}")

# First, reorder the labels using the position of each key in the dictionary
all_sequence_ids = list(genes_to_plot.keys()) # converts to list of sequence_ids 
ordered_labels = [] # empty list for labels
# Loop through each position 
for index in order:
    # Identify which sequence id is at that index
    seq_id = all_sequence_ids[index]
    # Add sequence id to list of labels
    ordered_labels.append(seq_id)

# reorder alignments according to list of orders
# this is a biotite Alignment object, rather than a normal list 
# Can use [:, order.tolist()] which will reorder the sequences while keeping the positions (each base) in the same place
ordered_alignments = alignment[:, order.tolist()]
```

## 3. Plot the alignment to visualise it

Now we can use `matplotlib` to take our alignment and plot it. 
There is a special biotite function for this. 

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create a matplotlib figure
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 6))

graphics.plot_alignment_type_based(
    # Get the current figure axes with .gca()
    plt.gca(),
    # Add the alignments
    ordered_alignments, 
    # Add the labels
    labels=ordered_labels,
    # Extra options for style
    color_scheme="blossom",
    symbols_per_line=60,
    symbol_size=10,
    label_size=9, 
    spacing=0.5
)

# Show the figure 
plt.show()
```
